trails.trailTip: Footing gets slick after rain on the bluff sections above the river, so trekking poles help on the descents; carry your own water since there are no fill stations along the route.
trails.didYouKnow: The bluffs offer some of the best views in the park of the Green River, the waterway responsible for carving much of the cave system below.

trails.trailTip: The descent into the sinkhole is on wooden stairs that can be slippery when wet or leaf-covered, so take the steps slowly, especially on the way back up.
trails.didYouKnow: Cedar Sink formed when the roof of an underground cave passage collapsed, exposing a stream that briefly surfaces before disappearing underground again.

trails.trailTip: The shelter cave itself is fenced off from entry to protect the site and visitors, since this is where a famous 1925 cave rescue attempt ended in tragedy — view it from the overlook rather than trying to go inside.
trails.didYouKnow: Sand Cave is the site of the 1925 death of Floyd Collins, whose entrapment here became a national media sensation.

trails.trailTip: A gentle out-and-back along the Green River to where cave water resurfaces — good for an easy add-on after a cave tour, with no significant elevation change.
trails.didYouKnow: Echo River, one of the cave system's underground rivers, resurfaces here after flowing unseen beneath the ridge above.

trails.trailTip: A short loop with interpretive signs near the historic entrance — a good option if you have limited time before or after a scheduled cave tour.
trails.didYouKnow: The historic entrance on this loop was used by 19th-century saltpeter miners and later by early cave tour guides, including enslaved guide Stephen Bishop.

trails.trailTip: One of the less-traveled loops in the park's surface backcountry, so let someone know your route and expected return time since cell coverage is patchy here.
trails.didYouKnow: This trail crosses a landscape riddled with sinkholes, a telltale sign of the karst cave system honeycombing the ground beneath it.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, overnight camping anywhere in the park's backcountry, including along Sal Hollow, requires a free backcountry permit obtained in advance from the park; day hiking itself needs no permit.
trails.didYouKnow: Sal Hollow is one of the longest above-ground trails in the park, traversing hardwood ridges far from the cave tour routes.

trails.trailTip: A quick walk to view another collapsed sinkhole from above; stay on the marked path since the sinkhole edges can be unstable.
trails.didYouKnow: This sinkhole formed above the same passage system that includes Mammoth Dome, one of the tallest vertical shafts in the cave.

animals.whereToLook: Roosts within cave passages; not viewable from surface trails
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per the National Park Service, gray bats are federally endangered and hit hard by white-nose syndrome; never enter closed caves or disturb a roost, and only view bats on a ranger-led tour where staff manage distance and decontamination protocols.
animals.didYouKnow: Gray bats roost almost exclusively in caves year-round, making them especially vulnerable to disturbance and to cave-dwelling diseases like white-nose syndrome.

animals.whereToLook: Forest floor along surface hiking trails
animals.viewingTip: If you see one crossing a trail, watch or step around it rather than picking it up — handling stresses the turtle and can spread pathogens between individuals.
animals.didYouKnow: Eastern box turtles can live 50 years or more and often use the same small home range for their entire lives.

animals.whereToLook: Woodlands throughout the park's surface trails
animals.viewingTip: Watch from the trail with binoculars; during the fall rut, keep extra distance from bucks, which can behave unpredictably around perceived rivals.
animals.didYouKnow: White-tailed deer communicate alarm by flashing the white underside of their tail as they flee, which is how they got their name.

animals.whereToLook: Damp rock near cave entrances and spring outlets
animals.viewingTip: Look, don't touch — their skin is highly permeable and sensitive to oils, sunscreen, and insect repellent on human hands.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite the name, cave salamanders spend most of their time in twilight zones near cave mouths rather than deep underground.

animals.viewingTip: Observe foraging flocks quietly from the trail; during spring nesting season give any hen with poults extra space rather than approaching for a closer look.
animals.didYouKnow: Wild turkeys were once nearly eliminated from Kentucky by overhunting and habitat loss before successful 20th-century reintroduction efforts.

animals.viewingTip: Rarely seen due to nocturnal habits; if you spot one at dusk near an entrance, observe quietly without shining a light directly at it for long periods.
animals.didYouKnow: Eastern woodrats, also called packrats, build large stick nests and are known for collecting shiny or unusual objects they find.

animals.bestSeason: Visible only on ranger-led cave tours with river access
animals.whereToLook: Underground streams within the cave system
animals.viewingTip: Only view cavefish from a boardwalk or boat on an official ranger-led tour, and never touch the water — this blind, pigmentless species is federally threatened and highly sensitive to contamination.
animals.didYouKnow: Northern cavefish are completely blind and lack pigment, having adapted over generations to a permanently lightless existence.

animals.whereToLook: Open fields and forest edges on the park's surface
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy distant howls or sightings from a trail or overlook; never approach or feed a coyote, which leads to dangerous habituation around people.
animals.didYouKnow: Coyotes expanded into Kentucky over the last century as wolves and larger predators were extirpated from the region.
